transcript.content: Hi, welcome in — I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess... what brought me in is that I keep hearing this man's voice. It comes right out of the garage vents at work, and sometimes straight from under the hood when I'm checking an engine. It is as clear as somebody standing right next to me, just talking. He keeps telling me not to trust my husband, and he tells me not to touch certain cars in the bay. 

Which is really hard because I'm a mechanic, you know? I have to touch the cars. I've been working on them since I took a few classes at the community college, back when they actually taught you how to feel a transmission slip instead of just plugging in an OBD2 scanner. Everyone relies on those scanners now. You just plug a computer in under the dash and read a code, and it takes all the actual skill out of the trade. My boss bought this new Snap-on scanner last month that cost like four grand, and it still doesn't tell you if a serpentine belt is actually frayed, you still have to use your own two eyes for that. I told him it was a waste of money. 

But anyway, yeah, the voice just... it tells me to stay away from certain cars and that my husband is up to something.
How long have you been hearing this man's voice — when did it first start?

Well, let's see... it's been about ten months now. Yeah, ten months of hearing him, and ten months since I figured out my husband is tracking me and up to something. 

Ten months ago would be... what, right around late fall? Yeah, because that's when everyone starts panicking and bringing their cars in to swap out their all-seasons for winter tires. People always wait way too long to do it. They wait until the very first snowstorm hits and then they're calling the shop at 7 AM expecting you to just magically fit them into the schedule when all the bays are already full. And the road salt they use around here just completely eats through the undercarriage if you don't wash it. I had this one Subaru Forester in right around that time, and the rust on the lower control arm was so bad I told the guy it wasn't even safe to drive off the lot. He didn't care though, people never want to pay for the actual fix, they just want to get back on the road. 

But anyway... yeah, it was right around that time when the voices and the tracking stuff started.
Over these past ten months, have you been using any alcohol, marijuana, or other recreational drugs?

No, no drugs or anything like that. I don't drink either. I used to have a beer after work sometimes, but honestly, it just makes me sleepy, and I can't afford to be off my game right now, especially with my husband doing whatever he's doing. Plus, alcohol dehydrates you, and working in the shop gets so hot, especially in the summer when the big bay doors are open but there's no breeze. We have these massive industrial fans, but they just push the hot air around. My coworker, Dave, he drinks like a fish, and he comes in hungover half the time. You can smell it sweating out of him when he's under a lift. I don't know how the boss hasn't fired him yet. He messed up a brake job last week—put the pads on backwards, if you can believe that. The customer made it about a block before the grinding noise started. Dave tried to blame it on the parts supplier, but I saw him do it. Anyway, yeah, no drugs or alcohol for me.
During these past ten months, have you also noticed periods where your mood was very low, hopeless, or on the other end, unusually high energy, elated, or needing little sleep?

Well, yeah... actually, I've had both, I guess. Like, sometimes I'll be flying high, just this massive rush of energy where I feel like I could fix every single car in town. I'll be in the zone, knocking out timing belts, head gaskets, you name it. It's like I don't even need sleep. But then... if my husband asks why the dishes aren't done, or if one of the other techs even touches my socket set—especially my 10mm, because those always go missing, everyone knows the 10mm is the first thing to vanish in any shop. I swear there's a black hole somewhere just full of 10mm sockets. I had to buy a specialized lockbox just for my ratchets because Dave keeps "borrowing" them and leaving them in the grease trap. 

But yeah, if someone moves my stuff or my husband gets on my case, I just... I blow up. I get so mad, like they're trying to hold me down or mess with my flow. It's just zero to a hundred. Which is dangerous in a shop, you know? You throw a wrench in anger and you could dent a customer's quarter panel, and then you're looking at a thousand-dollar paint matching job. The paint they use on these new cars, the pearlescent stuff? It's impossible to blend right. But anyway, yeah, I get really high energy and then just incredibly irritable.
During the times when your mood is neither unusually high nor low—when you're feeling more like your usual self—do you still hear the man's voice or still feel that your husband is tracking you?

Yeah, actually... there was a stretch a little while back, maybe a few weeks, where things were pretty quiet. Like, my mood was fine. I wasn't bouncing off the walls, I wasn't making all these massive plans to overhaul the shop's inventory system, and I was actually sleeping a normal amount. But even then... yeah, I still heard that man's voice in the garage. And I still knew my husband was tracking me. My boss too, actually. I know they're both in on it. 

Which, honestly, is why I started parking my truck around the back of the shop instead of in the front lot. The front lot is completely exposed to the street, and anyone driving by can see exactly who's there. Plus, the sun just bakes the asphalt out there in the afternoon. If you leave your car out there, the interior gets up to like 130 degrees. I had to replace the dashboard on this older Chevy Silverado last year because the sun damage had completely cracked the vinyl right down the middle. It's a huge pain to replace a dash, too. You have to take out the steering column, the radio, the climate controls, all the wiring harnesses... it's like a ten-hour job just to get the plastic shell out. And if you drop one of those tiny mounting screws down into the defroster vent? Forget it, it's gone forever, and it's going to rattle every time you turn the heat on. I always put a towel over my dash now, just in case. But yeah, even when I was feeling totally normal and sleeping fine, the voice was still there and I knew they were tracking me.

Thinking back over the whole 10 months, roughly how much of that time would you say you were having those high-energy or irritable mood swings, compared to the time you were feeling emotionally normal but still hearing the voice or feeling tracked?

Well, honestly, most of this past year has been completely taken over by those high-energy stretches. Like, I'm talking too fast, taking on way too much at the shop, and just feeling driven, like I physically cannot slow down. It's been the majority of the ten months, for sure. 

It's kind of like when a car's idle is set way too high. You know, you start the engine and it just revs, sitting there at like 2,500 RPMs when it should be resting under a thousand. We had a guy bring in an old Fox body Mustang a couple months ago that was doing exactly that. He had tried to adjust the throttle body himself, which, let me tell you, is almost always a mistake unless you really know what you're doing. People watch one YouTube video and suddenly think they're master mechanics. He had completely messed up the idle air control valve. The engine was just screaming in the bay, burning through gas just sitting at a stoplight. It took me three hours to recalibrate everything and get the vacuum lines sorted out because he'd cracked one of the old rubber hoses trying to pull it off. Those old hoses get so brittle, you look at them wrong and they snap. 

But yeah, that's what it feels like in my head. Just constantly revving, taking on every project, unable to just idle. So yeah, most of the year has been like that.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient endorses prominent auditory hallucinations (a male voice from vents/engines) and persecutory delusions (belief husband and boss are tracking her) persisting for 10 months. During most of this period she also displays manic symptoms (decreased need for sleep, increased energy, grandiosity about work capacity, irritability, distractibility). Critically, she confirms that during a several-week period when her mood was euthymic, the hallucinations and delusions persisted unabated, establishing that psychotic symptoms occur independently of mood episodes for a significant duration (≥2 weeks). She also confirms that the manic/mixed mood symptoms have been present for the majority of the total illness duration. This combination—concurrent mood episode and psychotic symptoms, plus psychotic symptoms occurring for a substantial period without mood symptoms, plus mood symptoms present for the majority of the illness—satisfies criteria for schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, rather than a primary mood disorder with psychotic features (mood episode too continuous relative to psychosis) or schizophrenia (mood symptoms occupy majority of illness course, not brief/incidental).
